extracted.intended_audience: Practitioners before the USPTO (trademark/patent attorneys), Office of Enrollment & Discipline (OED) personnel, and counsel involved in USPTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria used by the USPTO/OED and courts to determine whether a practitioner violated USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct and what sanctions are appropriate in disciplinary proceedings involving trademark practice and related misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competent representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.101)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner 'shall provide competent representation to a client.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to provide competent representation includes signing, or having non-practitioner assistants sign, trademark applications, declarations, and other filings on behalf of listed signatories in violation of USPTO signature regulations. Competence thus requires ensuring filings are accurate and properly executed before the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervision of non-practitioner assistants (37 C.F.R. § 11.503(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner having direct supervisory authority over the non-practitioner assistant shall make reasonable efforts to ensure that the person's conduct is compatible with the professional obligations of the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must reasonably supervise staff; allowing non-practitioner assistants to enter elements of another person's electronic signature or sign documents constitutes a violation. The practitioner remains ultimately responsible for assistants' conduct even if unaware of misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct for a practitioner to 'engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit or misrepresentation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include entering electronic signatures of clients or others, directing assistants to enter signatures not their own, or otherwise submitting falsified documents to the USPTO. Such conduct supports findings of professional misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct for a practitioner to 'engage in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitting forged signatures or directing others to submit them on applications and declarations filed with the USPTO undermines the administration of justice and constitutes misconduct under this provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee division requirements (37 C.F.R. § 11.105(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: A division of a fee between practitioners who are not in the same firm may be made only if: (1) the division is in proportion to the services performed by each practitioner or each practitioner assumes joint responsibility; (2) the client agrees to the arrangement, including the share each practitioner will receive, and the agreement is confirmed in writing; and (3) the total fee is reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dividing fees with practitioners not in the same firm without obtaining the client's written agreement to the arrangement (including the share) and ensuring the fee's reasonableness violates this rule. Produce written confirmations when fee-splitting arrangements exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness and cooperation with disciplinary investigations (37 C.F.R. § 11.801(a) & (b))
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A practitioner in connection with a disciplinary ... matter, shall not ... [k]nowingly make a false statement of material fact' and shall cooperate with disciplinary investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing false or misleading information to OED, failing to respond to lawful requests for information (RFIs), failing to produce documents (or provide a privilege log/redacted copies), or otherwise impeding investigation violations these rules. Examples: false assertions that clients or assistants signed filings, claiming lost email data without substantiation, or ignoring RFIs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowingly failing to respond to lawful demands (37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule proscribes, among other things, knowingly failing to respond to a lawful demand or request for information from a disciplinary authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to answer RFIs within the prescribed time, not producing requested records, or otherwise refusing to comply with lawful investigatory demands constitutes a separate violation and aggravating conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence obligation (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner has an ethical obligation to act with reasonable diligence in representing a client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diligence includes taking reasonable steps to ensure trademark filings comply with USPTO signature rules and adequately supervising non-practitioner assistants. Practitioners cannot avoid responsibility by blaming employees; failure to monitor staff and ensure correct signing/filing practices constitutes neglect and supports discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to remedy or disclose known falsity (37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a) and § 11.103(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must not offer evidence known to be false and, if a practitioner learns that material evidence is false, must take reasonable remedial measures, including, if necessary, disclosure to the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a practitioner knows a filed declaration or signature is falsified (or that someone engaged in fraudulent conduct relating to a trademark application), the practitioner must take remedial steps such as disclosure. Failure to do so risks disciplinary sanction and potential harm to clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature compliance with USPTO trademark electronic signature regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark filings and accompanying declarations must be signed in accordance with USPTO signature rules; named signatories must personally execute required signature elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directly entering or having assistants enter electronic signatures of clients or other named signatories is improper. Practitioners must ensure signatories personally sign or otherwise comply with the Office's electronic signature procedures; forging or directing forgery of signatures is misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility and limitations to practice trademark matters before the USPTO (37 C.F.R. § 11.1 and § 11.14)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only attorneys as defined in § 11.1 (active members in good standing of the bar of a state's highest court) may represent others before the Office in trademark and other non-patent matters, except for limited reciprocal recognition of foreign attorneys/agents under § 11.14(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign-domiciled trademark applicants and counsel have specific reciprocal-recognition rules; practitioners must comply with limitations (e.g., working with a U.S.-licensed attorney). Violating eligibility rules (e.g., representing non-residents outside allowed exceptions) can constitute misconduct and breach of USPTO practice rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning factors for determining appropriate discipline (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining an appropriate sanction, the Court must consider: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty owed to a client, the public, the legal system, or the profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of the actual or potential injury caused by the practitioner's conduct; and (4) the existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these four factors collectively to determine sanction severity. The decision cites prior USPTO disciplinary precedents to assess these elements (e.g., intentionality, scope of harm, pattern of infractions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating and mitigating factors (ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions § 9.22 cited)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggravating factors include, among others: a dishonest or selfish motive; a pattern of misconduct; multiple violations; bad faith obstruction of the disciplinary proceeding by intentionally failing to comply with rules or orders; and substantial experience in the practice of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of one or more of these aggravators supports a more severe sanction. Examples provided: repeated forgeries across clients (pattern), failing to respond to RFIs and not filing an Answer (bad faith obstruction), submission of false evidence or multiple accounts to investigators (false statements/aggravator). Mitigating factors (not detailed in the chunk) may reduce sanctions if shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of potential or actual injury (harm to clients and the profession)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the amount of actual or potential injury: falsified filings can lead to cancellation of trademarks and other harm to clients; failure to cooperate undermines disciplinary system and public trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significant potential injury includes risk that trademarks obtained via falsified documents will be cancelled, competitors may challenge marks, and clients' interests are jeopardized. Also consider harm to the profession's integrity when practitioners lie or obstruct investigations.
